next.name: Threat Group-3390
next.headline: Threat Group-3390 (APT27, Emissary Panda): a long-running espionage group, as vendors describe it
next.in_short: Threat Group-3390 goes by many names, including APT27 and Emissary Panda. Vendors and a German agency describe a China-based espionage actor that uses watering holes, unpatched servers and tools such as PlugX and HyperBro.

sentences.t: Threat Group-3390 is also tracked as Earth Smilodon, TG-3390, Emissary Panda, BRONZE UNION, APT27, Iron Tiger, LuckyMouse and Linen Typhoon.
Dell SecureWorks researchers designated the group Threat Group 3390 and nicknamed it Emissary Panda. The article says the group is believed to be based in China.
Symantec uses the name Budworm and lists LuckyMouse, Emissary Panda and APT27 as aliases. Its report says the group is believed to have been active since at least 2013.
Germany's Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV) describes APT27 as a Chinese cyberespionage group.
Microsoft Threat Intelligence describes Linen Typhoon as a Chinese nation-state actor. It says the actor has focused on stealing intellectual property since 2012.
SecureWorks said most targets were in the automotive, electronic, aerospace, energy and pharmaceutical industries. It said at least 50 organizations in the US and the United Kingdom had data stolen.
The same reporting lists defense contractors, universities, law firms and political organizations among the targets.

Symantec says Budworm often focuses on government, technology and defense organizations. In August 2023 it used an updated SysUpdate backdoor against a Middle Eastern telecommunications organization and an Asian government.
The BfV says APT27 has repeatedly attacked German companies since at least March 2021.

In the 2015 SecureWorks account, the group broke into networks largely through watering hole attacks launched from over 100 compromised websites. It used old vulnerabilities rather than zero-days, plus the PlugX remote access tool.
The BfV says the 2021 attacks exploited unpatched, internet-exposed servers. Flaws in Microsoft Exchange and Zoho ManageEngine ADSelfService Plus were used to install HyperBro malware.
A Malpedia entry says HyperBro typically has three or more components. These include a genuine loader and an encrypted, compressed payload with its command-and-control details built in.

Symantec reports that Budworm runs SysUpdate through DLL sideloading. It also uses living-off-the-land and publicly available tools such as AdFind and SecretsDump to map networks and dump credentials.
The catalogue record lists tools tied to the group, including PlugX, HyperBro, Cobalt Strike, Mimikatz, China Chopper and Impacket.
SecureWorks unveiled its report on the group at the Black Hat conference. It was published on 5 August 2015.
Microsoft says Linen Typhoon, Violet Typhoon and Storm-2603 exploited on-premises SharePoint flaws. It says attempts may have begun as early as 7 July 2025.

Attribution is not always settled. An eSentire report notes FireEye said it had not seen Emissary Panda activity since 2015. It also says FireEye suggested some 2019 SharePoint campaigns may be run by UNC215, with uncertain ties to Emissary Panda.

Kaspersky's GReAT team says several companies attribute the DRBControl backdoor to APT27. It says code from that backdoor was likely used to build the PlugY implant seen in the EastWind campaign against Russian organizations.
Patch internet-facing servers quickly and watch them for web shells, since much of the reported activity began with unpatched systems.
